# R5 Digest — Joseph Story Gen 37:1–43:34 (raw lines 4861–6430)
**Coverage:** Full slice read (cache lines 1–1570 = raw 4861–6430). Hamilton NICOT Genesis 18–50 commentary: IV. The Joseph Story (37:1–50:26) through sections A–G: A. Joseph sold into slavery (37); B. Judah and Tamar (38); C. Joseph in Potiphar’s house (39); D. Jail dreams (40); E. High office in Egypt (41); F. Brothers to Egypt (42); G. Return with Benjamin (43). NT Appropriation of Joseph narrative deferred to after ch. 50. Slice ends at end of 43:34 (banquet with Benjamin); does **not** include chs. 44–50 or 50:20 proper.

**Source attribution:** All claims below are Hamilton’s positions/readings in this range unless noted as his report of other scholars.

## Claims

### Group A — Macrostructure of the Joseph Story; Toledot Frame (37:1–2)

### C-V2R5-01 | Joseph story opens under Jacob’s toledot; content preponderantly Joseph
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Although 37:2a titles everything “the story of Jacob,” the data are preponderantly about Joseph; Simeon, Judah, Benjamin appear only as they relate to Joseph. Seventeen years have passed since Joseph’s birth (30:23–24); life obscure until now.
- **Quote:** "Although everything in 37:2b and following is titled as the story of Jacob (37:2a), it is obvious that the data is preponderantly about Joseph. Bits and pieces appear about Simeon, Judah, and Benjamin, but only as they relate to Joseph."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:2 / slice ~ll. 40–41
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[joseph]], [[jacob]], [[toledot]]

### C-V2R5-02 | Jacob settles (yāšab) vs Isaac sojourns (gûr); false hope of eventless retirement
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** For Isaac Canaan was land for sojourning (*gûr*); for Jacob place of settlement (*yāšab*). If Jacob expects eventless retirement after trials, he is about to be “rudely awakened.”
- **Quote:** "For Isaac Canaan was a land for sojourning (gûr). For Jacob it was a place of settlement (yāšab). Perhaps Jacob has seen the last of his many trials and setbacks. Perhaps he is now ready for an eventless retirement in Canaan. If he is thinking that, then he is about to be rudely awakened."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:1 / slice ~ll. 38–39
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-03 | Possible anticipatory paronomasia: Joseph “shepherding” brothers as ruling
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Hebrew syntax allows “Joseph was shepherding his brothers” if *’et* is accusative; *rā‘â ’et* can mean “rule over” (2 Sam 5:2; 7:7). What Joseph does as teen anticipates adult life — caring/providing for dependents; brothers later ask if he intends to *mālak*/*māšal* (v. 8).
- **Quote:** "The syntax of the Hebrew allows for the translation “Joseph was shepherding his brothers,” if ‘et is understood as the sign of the accusative rather than as the preposition “with.” So understood, this verse would provide an excellent introduction to the Joseph story in the form of anticipatory paranomasia. What Joseph is doing during his teen life is exactly what he will be doing in his adult life — caring and providing for those who are dependent on him."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:2 / slice ~ll. 42–43
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### Group B — A. Sold into Slavery: Dreams, Coat, Conspiracy (37:1–24)

### C-V2R5-04 | Joseph’s *dibbâ rā‘â*: bad report; parallel to spies’ report of the land
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Joseph “maligned” brothers with *dibbâ rā‘â* — whispering of hostile people (Ps 31:14; Jer 20:10); closest parallel Num 13–14 spies’ bad report of the land.
- **Quote:** "For some undisclosed reason, Joseph maligned his brothers to Jacob. To describe Joseph’s malignment of his brothers the narrator uses dibbâ rā‛â. … The closest parallel to its use in Gen. 37:2 is Num. 13:32; 14:36, 37 to refer to the bad report of the land that the returning spies spread (yāsā’) throughout the camp."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:2 / slice ~ll. 44–45
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-05 | *Ketōnet passîm*: long colorful tunic; multicolored vs ankle-length; ANE dress parallels
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** AV “coat of many colors” from LXX/Vulg.; alternate “long robe with sleeves” from Aquila / postbiblical *pas* (palm/sole) and 2 Sam 13:18. Mendenhall’s Ugaritic *pad* (melammū glory/status) rejected on phonology. Speiser’s Akk. *kitu pišannu* and Mari multicolored sari-like garment offer early-date support. Beni-hasan tomb painting (~1800 B.C.) and Zimri-Lim Mari fresco cited.
- **Quote:** "The source of AV “coat of many colors” is LXX chitōna poikílon, “a multicolored frock,” and Vulg. tunicam polymitam. The source behind RSV “a long robe with sleeves” is Aquila’s rendering of passîm by astrágalōn, “(a frock) reaching to the ankles).” … The parallel between the Mari garment and Joseph’s ketōnet passîm argues, indirectly at least, for an early date for the Joseph story."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:3 / slice ~ll. 50–78
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-06 | Favoritism as doting love; Jacob repeats schism he himself suffered
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Jacob’s love is doting; he knew schism from parental favoritism yet proceeds. Joseph as “child of advanced age” surprising (Benjamin is last); Rachel’s only happy birthing ending.
- **Quote:** "Jacob’s love for Joseph is a doting love. Surely he was aware of the potential for friction in a family where parental favoritism was blatant. He knew personally the schism that results from such tactics. Nevertheless, he proceeds to make clear to all his preferential concern for Joseph."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:3 / slice ~ll. 46–49
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-07 | Resentment possibly against Jacob as well as Joseph
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Syntax allows “him” despised (v. 4) to be Jacob; doting and gift equally offensive; brothers have spoken harshly to father before (34:31).
- **Quote:** "Hebrew syntax would allow for the possibility that the him the brothers despised and with whom they could not speak peaceably could be Jacob their father. His doting over Joseph was as offensive to them as was his gift to Joseph of the robe."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:4 / slice ~ll. 80–81
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-08 | First non-theophanic dreams in Genesis; ambiguity hubris vs prophecy
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** First Genesis dream without God’s voice — not theophany; ambiguity: hubris or prophecy? Baker/cupbearer and Pharaoh dreams resemble Joseph’s, not Jacob/Abimelech/Laban. Narrator not upset with Joseph; brothers are. Dream = unsuspecting prophecy of destiny; sheaf/food foreshadows famine motif.
- **Quote:** "This is the first dream recorded in Genesis in which the voice of God does not speak, thus removing it from the category of a theophany. The absence of any specific divine speech or revelation in the dream accentuates its ambiguity. Is the dream an exhibition of hubris or is it a prophecy? … More than likely, the dream, and its recounting, is to be understood as an unsuspecting prophecy uttered by Joseph. God has a plan for his life, a destiny in his future, and Joseph spontaneously shares the enthusiasm that revelation spawns."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:5–8 / slice ~ll. 88–90
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[divine-providence]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-09 | *Wayyôsipû* / Joseph name-play; *mālak*/*māšal*; Ibn Ezra distinction
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** *Wayyôsipû* “added” plays on Joseph (*yôsēp*). Brothers read dream as future subordination. Hamilton: *mālak*/*māšal* essentially synonymous; Ibn Ezra: *mālak* = appointed kingship, *māšal* = tyrant usurpation.
- **Quote:** "The use of the verbal form wayyôsipû for added in the clause “but added to their hate for him” in vv. 5 and 8 is a play on the name Joseph (yôsēp). … I am inclined to see these two verbs as essentially synonymous; but Ibn Ezra, the medieval Jewish commentator, was the first to suggest that mālak refers to appointed kingship, while māšal refers to the usurpation of power by a tyrant."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:5–8 / slice ~ll. 84–92
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-10 | Second dream: Benjamin already born; “mother” = Leah as stepmother
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Eleven stars = twelve brothers total → Benjamin born (post-35:18). Jacob’s “your mother” after Rachel’s death (35:19): not necessarily different tradition; more likely Leah as stepmother of Benjamin and Joseph. Jacob rebukes (*gā‘ar*) but ponders like Mary (Luke 2:19, 51).
- **Quote:** "This verse indicates that Benjamin is born by this time, for there are twelve brothers involved, and therefore the dream cannot have occurred before 35:18. … Or, more likely, with the passing of Rachel, Leah has become the stepmother of Benjamin and Joseph. … As with Mary, who, when she was confronted with a situation half-plausible and half-incredulous, pondered it in her heart (Luke 2: 19,51), so too Jacob will not jump to conclusions but will give the matter more serious reflection."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:9–11 / slice ~ll. 94–100
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[jacob]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-11 | Three escalating causes of fraternal hatred; not three source traditions
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Anger from (1) maligning (v. 2), (2) favoritism (vv. 3–4), (3) dreams (vv. 5–12) — escalation of animosity, not three separate traditions. Continues Isaac–Ishmael / Jacob–Esau pattern.
- **Quote:** "No less than three reasons have surfaced for the anger of Joseph’s brothers against him: (1) his maligning some of them (v. 2); (2) the obvious favoritism lavished on him by his father (vv. 3-4); (3) his insistence on sharing his seemingly pompous dreams (vv. 5-12). These three actions do not necessarily indicate three different traditions behind the Joseph story … Rather, the three instances illustrate the escalation of the deeply entrenched animosity against Joseph."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:9–11 / slice ~ll. 102–103
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-12 | Hebron–Shechem–Dothan geography; MB occupation; anonymous man as transition
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** ~65 miles Hebron→Dothan; sons must be distant else mission senseless. Emendation and J/E northern-localities theories unnecessary. Archaeology: Shechem and Dothan occupied in Middle Bronze (Joseph’s time). Anonymous *’îš* redirects Joseph; transition from love/acceptance to hostility/rejection.
- **Quote:** "Archaeology has confirmed that both of these Canaanite towns — Shechem and Dothan — were occupied in the time of Joseph (i.e., the Middle Bronze Age). This evidence lends plausibility to the geographical referents of the Joseph story. … The chance encounter with this anonymous man provides a transition from Joseph’s association with his father to Joseph’s association with his brothers, from an environment of love, acceptance, and maybe even doting, to one of hostility and rejection."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:12–17 / slice ~ll. 124–137
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-13 | *Ba‘al hahalōmôṯ* = sarcastic “master dreamer”; later ironic title (chs. 40–41)
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Translates *ba‘al hahalōmôṯ* “master dreamer” to preserve sarcasm; later appropriate for dream-interpreter Joseph. Von Rad: “one empowered to prophetic dreams.” Brothers target dreams especially.
- **Quote:** "I translate ba‘al hahalōmôṯ (lit., “master of dreams”) as master dreamer to indicate that in the mouths of his brothers such a designation is blatantly sarcastic. … Heaped on Joseph as a scornful phrase, the expression will later be an appropriate title for Joseph (chs. 40 and 41), who will emerge as master and interpreter of the dreams of others."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:19–20 / slice ~ll. 162–163
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-14 | Reuben’s cistern plan: oldest-brother duty; blood-guilt avoidance; empty well foreshadows famine
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Reuben modifies plan: alive in wilderness cistern to snatch and restore him — likely oldest-brother duty (not primarily rehabilitating Bilhah scandal). *Habbôr req* anticipates seven empty ears (41:27); Joseph will be to brothers what Reuben desired to be to Joseph.
- **Quote:** "It is more likely that he is here exercising the role of the oldest brother, the one who is most answerable to his father for the well-being of his beloved Joseph. … Joseph’s cistern may provide an early parallel for the famine that wipes out Canaan later in the Joseph story. The habbôr req (“the empty well”) anticipates the “seven empty ears” (šeḇa‛ haššibbolîm hārēqôṯ, 41:27) which represent the seven famine years. And what Reuben desires to be to Joseph, Joseph will be to his brothers."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:21–24 / slice ~ll. 170–185
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[divine-providence]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### Group C — A. Midianites/Ishmaelites Sale; Hamilton’s Unity Reading (37:25–36)

### C-V2R5-15 | Judah’s sale proposal less noble than Reuben’s; capital crime vs biblical/cuneiform law
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Judah fears blood-cry (Gen 4:10 etc.), not rescue; sale to strangers irretrievable; proposes silver payment (crime capital under biblical and cuneiform law). Motives not as noble as Reuben’s.
- **Quote:** "Judah’s motives, however, are not as noble as those of Reuben. Judah is primarily concerned that he and his brothers not shed innocent blood (v. 26). … There is no indication that Judah really desires to rescue his brother, as there was with Reuben. Joseph could be retrieved from a cistern, but he cannot be retrieved once he is sold to strangers headed for a foreign land. … Both later biblical law and cuneiform law prohibit what Judah and his brothers did to Joseph. It is a crime that is considered a capital offense."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:25–27 / slice ~ll. 204–207
- **Targets:** [[judah]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-16 | Twenty shekels = Old Babylonian average slave price; age-fit with Lev 27:5
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Twenty pieces of silver = average male-slave price early 2nd millennium OB; rises later (Nuzi 30, Ugarit 40, Neo-Bab 50, Persian 90–120). Fits Lev 27:5 valuation for males 5–20 (Joseph is 17).
- **Quote:** "Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver to these traders. This was the average price for a male slave in Old Babylonian times (early 2nd millennium B.C.). The price gradually goes higher. … Joseph’s sale for twenty shekels fits perfectly with the amount a man was to give to the sanctuary if he vows himself or one of his male relatives between the ages of five and twenty (Joseph is seventeen) to the Lord (Lev. 27:5)."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:28 / slice ~ll. 208–209
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-17 | Midianites/Ishmaelites: overlapping terms, not J/E conflation; brothers are subject of “pulled up…sold”
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Against J (Judah/Ishmaelites) vs E (Reuben/Midianites) split: Judg 8:22–28 shows Midianite/Ishmaelite overlapping; “Ishmaelite” = generic Bedouin caravan, “Midianite” = more specific ethnic term when group comes into focus. Parallel progression of observation in vv. 18–24 and 25–28. Subject of “pulled up” and “sold” (v. 28) = brothers. Reuben absent during sale → shock at empty well. Literary unity argued (Rudolph; Sandmel, Coats, Greenstein, Berlin, White).
- **Quote:** "These traders are identified as Midianites and Ishmaelite. Judg. 8:22- 28 state clearly that Midianite and Ishmaelite are overlapping, identical terms. … Thus “Ishmaelite” is the more generic term (Bedouin nomad), while “Midianite” is the more specific and ethnic term. … This interpretation raises considerably the possibility that the subject of “pulled up” and “sold” in v. 28 is the brothers. … Enough has been said to indicate that recourse to a J-E hypothesis, or to an original story with later redactional expansions, is not the only option in order to make sense of Gen. 37. The older study of Rudolph, and more recent narrative readings by Sandmel, Coats, Greenstein, Berlin, and White, argue convincingly for the literary unity of Gen. 37."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:25–30 / slice ~ll. 210–226
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[judah]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]]

### C-V2R5-18 | “Sold” (45:4) vs “stolen” (40:15): tactical self-presentation, not dual tradition
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Joseph later says brothers “sold” him (45:4) but told cell mate he was “stolen” (40:15) — not J/E dual tradition; deliberate adjustment to curry cupbearer’s favor and stress innocence/no control.
- **Quote:** "It is quite probable that Joseph deliberately adjusted the story as he narrated it in ch. 40, for he was attempting to curry the cupbearer’s favor. … To have mentioned that he was sold by his brothers would make the cupbearer suspicious, rather than trusting. By saying he was stolen, Joseph is underscoring that what happened to him was something over which he had no control, and which he, in his judgment, had done nothing to deserve."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:29–30 (looking ahead to 40:15; 45:4) / slice ~ll. 222–223
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-19 | Jacob deceived by goat blood as he once deceived Isaac; simultaneous mourning/sale syntax
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Ironic: Jacob who deceived Isaac with kids’ skins (27:16) now deceived by goat-blood tunic. Sons’ “your son’s tunic” distances them. Jacob concludes *ḥayyâ rā‘â* (same phrase as brothers planned); formal verse on death. Juxtaposed subjects “his father and the Midianites” stress simultaneous mourning and sale (Alter). *Medānîm* / Midianites may pun “discord among brothers” (Prov 6:19).
- **Quote:** "It is ironic that Jacob, who earlier deceived Isaac with ‘ōrōt hā‛izzîm (“skin of the kids”) in 27:16, is now deceived by a garment dipped in the blood of a goat (śe‘îr ‛izzîm). … Alter states: “In this cunningly additive syntax, on the same unbroken narrative continuum in which Jacob is mourning his supposedly devoured son, Midianites are selling the living lad.” … At the heart of the trouble in Gen. 37 is discord among brothers, meḏānîm."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:31–36 / slice ~ll. 250–268
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-20 | Jacob’s Sheol descent; Ugaritic Baal-Mot parallel; ritual descent option
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** “I will go down to my son in Sheol mourning” — later Joseph goes down (*’ērēḏ*) to Egypt. Ugaritic Latipan after Baal’s death: “After Baal I would go down into the earth” — may imply ritual descent, not lifelong mourning until death. No heaven concept; underworld unpleasant for all.
- **Quote:** "If the connection of Gen. 37:35 with the above Ugaritic text can be maintained, then the verse may not imply that Jacob will mourn for Joseph the rest of his life until he himself goes down to Sheol. Rather, v. 35 would suggest that Jacob will make a ritual descent into the underworld."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:35 / slice ~ll. 262–265

### Group D — B. Judah and Tamar (38:1–30)

### C-V2R5-22 | Ch. 38 placement: only logical chronological/literary slot; 13-year window
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Ch. 38 interrupts Joseph flow (39:1 resumes 37:36) but only place chronologically possible: cannot precede Joseph story (Judah single in ch. 37; married with sons in 38); cannot follow end (Judah goes to Egypt and stays). Fits 13 years between sale (age 17) and exaltation (age 30).
- **Quote:** "In the thirteen-year period between Joseph’s being sold to caravaneers and his exaltation in the pharaoh’s service (cf. Joseph’s age of 17 in 37:2 and and 30 in 41:46) falls Judah’s marriage, the birth of his three sons, and the fathering of two (grand)children to his daughter-in-law."
- **Locus:** Intro to ch. 38 / slice ~ll. 316–321
- **Targets:** [[judah]], [[tamar]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-23 | Linguistic and thematic parallels bind 37–38–39
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Linguistic: *hakker-nā’* / *nāḵar* (37:32–33 // 38:25–26); goat (*śe‘îr/geḏî ‛izzîm*); *yrd* “went down” Judah / “taken down” Joseph; *nḥm* consolation (Jacob refused / Judah consoled). Thematic: deception (bloodied coat / Tamar as harlot / Potiphar’s wife); evidence-as-proof; Tamar seductress vs Potiphar’s wife; Joseph’s dream of rule vs Judah’s royal line; fraternal rivalry; primogeniture set aside (Joseph; Perez → messianic line Ruth 4:18; Matt 1:3).
- **Quote:** "Two back-to-back uses of the Hiphil imperative of nāḵar (37:32; 38:25) and of the Hiphil imperfect of nāḵar (37:33; 38:26) unite these two chapters. … Tamar the seductress balances Potiphar’s wife the seductress, and the seduced Judah contrasts with the chaste Joseph. … In ch. 37 Joseph has a dream which provokes this question: Shall you rule over us? and the rest of the Joseph story shows Joseph, so to speak, ruling over his brethren. In ch. 38 the focus is on Judah out of whose line will come the kings who will rule over God’s people."
- **Locus:** Intro to ch. 38 / slice ~ll. 323–324
- **Targets:** [[judah]], [[tamar]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-24 | Rabbinic *measure-for-measure* on kid and *hakker-nā’*
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Early rabbinic observation: God to Judah — you deceived father with kid / *hakker-nā’*; Tamar will deceive you with kid / *hakker-nā’*.
- **Quote:** "It may be noted that the play on nāḵar and ‘izzîm in chs. 37 and 38 was observed as early as Jewish rabbinic literature: “The Holy One, Praised be He, said to Judah, ‘You deceived your father with a kid. By your life Tamar will deceive you with a kid’.... The Holy One, Praised be He, said to Judah, ‘You said to your father, hakker-nā’. By your life Tamar will say to you, hakker-nā’.”"
- **Locus:** Intro to ch. 38 / slice ~ll. 323
- **Targets:** [[judah]], [[tamar]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Judah’s Canaanite wife (Shua’s daughter) contrasts Abraham (24:3) and Isaac (28:1) against Canaanite spouses; post-Dinah, Jacob has less control over family.

### C-V2R5-26 | Er first individual Yahweh kills; Onan’s coitus interruptus not “onanism”/masturbation
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Er first individual Yahweh kills (*wayemiṯēhû*); sin unspecified (not central). Onan: coitus interruptus, not masturbation — “onanism” etymology misleading. Compounded sins: refused levirate, persistent (*whenever*), inheritance self-interest (Num 27:8–11), subterfuge (faked duty). Cost him life.
- **Quote:** "Er is the first individual in Scripture whom Yahweh kills (wayemiṯēhû). … This is clearly a reference to withdrawal to prevent conception, rather than a reference to masturbation. Thus the etymological connection of “onanism” (in the sense of masturbation) with Onan’s name is misleading. … Fourth, what makes Onan’s sin so offensive is that he appears to undertake his responsibility, but he fakes it."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 38:7–10 / slice ~ll. 340–350

### C-V2R5-27 | Levirate: Gen 38 focuses offspring not marriage; later Deut 25; persists into NT
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Judah says “go in to” not “marry”; Tamar’s entitlement = male son, not marriage (vs Deut 25:5–10 both duties). Levirate into Jesus’ day (Matt 22:23–30 par.). Sending Tamar home makes later intercourse adultery (betrothed to Shelah).
- **Quote:** "Thus, unlike Deut. 25:5-10, which addresses both the brother-in-law’s duties and marriage for the childless wife, Gen. 38:8 speaks only of the first of these. Tamar remains Onan’s sister-in law; she does not become his wife. This point makes clear that Tamar’s legitimate entitlement extends only to a male son, not to marriage. … This makes Judah’s intercourse with Tamar later on adultery."

- **Locus:** Comm. on 42:21–24 / slice ~ll. 1272–1293
- **Targets:** [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-54 | Money discovery: God-instrument via Joseph; two-discovery tension not J-intrusion
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** “What is this that God has done to us?” — what they attribute to God perpetrated by Joseph; Joseph vehicle of facing reality (building to 50:19). Against clumsy J-intrusion: one brother opens sack en route; all empty before Jacob; 43:21 compresses; or moral-psychological vs theological-historical axes (Alter). Link to sale money.
- **Quote:** "The reader knows that it is Joseph who has done this. What they attribute to God has been perpetrated by Joseph. Without their knowledge, Joseph has been the vehicle God is using to bring these brothers to face reality. Joseph is not himself God, as he asserts in 50:19, but he is God’s instrument."

### C-V2R5-55 | Report to Jacob sanitized; first accusation “you made me childless”; Reuben’s two sons rejected
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Brothers soften Joseph’s terms, omit three-day prison, spy repetitions, money discovery, Reuben’s reproach. After money pouches found, Jacob: “Me have you made childless” — first time he accuses sons (ch. 37 blamed wild beast only). Pattern: leave home, return minus brother + extra silver. Reuben offers two sons’ lives — foolish, not therapeutic; Jacob refuses Benjamin, “he alone remains” (of Rachel).
- **Quote:** "This is the first time Jacob accuses his sons. There was not even a hint in ch. 37 that he suspected foul play on their part. … Each time (chs. 37 and 42) Jacob’s sons have left home, they have returned to their father minus a brother (Joseph, Simeon), but with extra silver in their possession. … Reuben’s offer of his two sons if he fails to bring back Benjamin from Egypt is hardly therapeutic."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 42:29–38 / slice ~ll. 1352–1378

### C-V2R5-56 | Sheol in Genesis Joseph cycle: death-condition of dejected righteous, sphere vague
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** *Še’ôl* often “netherworld” (no article, 65×); usually destiny of wicked; Gen 37:35; 42:38; 44:29, 31 rare for righteous. For Jacob: state/condition of death into which dejected enters (“great beyond”), permanence not determinable from Genesis alone.
- **Quote:** "Gen. 37:35; 42:38 (both spoken by Jacob); and 44:29, 31 (Judah’s quoting Jacob to Joseph) are among the rare passages that speak of a righteous person descending to Sheol. It is likely that in these Genesis passages, all involving Jacob, one should consider Sheol as denoting the state or condition of death into which the dejected Jacob will enter, without the sphere of that existence being any more definitely defined than that to which one “descends,” much like our equally vague “the great beyond” or “afterworld.”"
- **Locus:** Comm. on 42:38 / slice ~ll. 1376–1378

### Group I — G. Return with Benjamin (43:1–34)

### C-V2R5-57 | Judah as spokesman: surety of own life vs Reuben’s grandsons; Israel as clan head
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Judah steps forward; will not usurp father but places onus (starve with Benjamin vs release him). Offers self as *‘āraḇ* surety — own life on line (vs Reuben’s two sons). “Israel” here = clan head directing second trip, invoking El Shaddai (not source marker). *Na‘ar* for Benjamin stresses vulnerability/fraternal bond.
- **Quote:** "Judah’s proposal differs from that of Reuben. The latter was willing to put the lives of two of his sons on the line (42:37). Judah is prepared to place his own life on the line. … It is as “Israel” that he thus functions in ch. 43."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 43:1–10 / slice ~ll. 1416–1436
- **Targets:** [[judah]], [[jacob]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-58 | Gifts, double money, El Shaddai mercy; resignation formula
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** *Minḥâ* of choicest products (balm, honey, gum, myrrh, pistachios, almonds) — protocol not appeasement (unlike Esau gift). Recalls Ishmaelite cargo (37:25). Double money for honesty. El Shaddai invoked (17:1; 28:3; 35:11; blessing/covenant name) for mercy = return of other brother + Benjamin. “If I am bereaved, bereaved I shall be” // Est 4:16 resignation. Final decision God’s, not Judah’s or “the man’s.”
- **Quote:** "It is fitting, therefore, that Jacob invokes El Shaddai (see 17:1; 28:3; 35:11; 49:25 [perhaps]; Exod. 6:3). In each of these passages that do refer to El Shaddai, he is a deity who is blessing, making promises and covenants, and revealing himself. … Jacob’s if I am to be bereaved, bereaved I shall be is the same construction as Esther’s “if I perish, I perish” (Est. 4:16) … He does believe, however, that El Shaddai will be the one to make the final decision about the destiny of Benjamin. Neither Judah nor “the man” has that authority."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 43:11–14 / slice ~ll. 1454–1466
- **Targets:** [[jacob]], [[judah]], [[divine-providence]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R5-59 | Brothers fear hospitality as trap; steward’s answer: God put treasure — providence ambiguity
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Kinship terms drop to “the men.” Fear dinner = entrapment into slavery — precisely what they did to Joseph. Steward’s “Your God and the God of your father must have put a treasure in your bags” (Joseph’s instructed answer) — dark ambiguity of “God’s concealed guidance” (von Rad). What steward attributes to God, Joseph ordered (42:25); Joseph later “am I in the place of God?” (50:19) apropos here. Simeon released; little recorded joy.
- **Quote:** "It does not take much imagination to see that what the brothers fear might happen to them at the hands of Joseph — he wants to overpower us and seize us, and take us into slavery — is precisely what they once did to Joseph. … “Its [viz., the steward’s response] dark ambiguity touches the innermost mystery of the whole Joseph story: God’s concealed guidance,” … while the steward states that it is God who has put the treasure in their bags, we know that it was Joseph who gave orders that the silver be returned to the sacks (42:25)."

### C-V2R5-60 | Banquet: *šālôm* burst; age-ordered seating; Benjamin’s fivefold portion; Egyptian table taboo
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Bowing recalls dreams; *šālôm* burst contrasts 37:4 inability to speak peaceably. Blesses Benjamin “May God be gracious… my son” (role-play elder). Deeply moved for full brother; weeps privately. Three tables: Egyptian cultic taboo against eating with Hebrews (ANE Egypt note). Seated by birth order → astonishment (hints identity). Benjamin’s multi-portion // Joseph’s coat — symbolic favor (cf. Dan 1; Est 2). Convivial feast: “drank and got drunk with him” (Speiser: not necessarily indecorous).
- **Quote:** "Earlier the brothers could not speak to each other in peace, but now when they speak to each other there is “a veritable burst of šalôms.” … For a second time Joseph is separated from his brothers at meal time (see 37:25 for the first). But he is no helpless occupant of an empty cistern this time. … Joseph received the extra coat; Benjamin receives the extra portion. … Speiser observes that the phrase depicts “a convivial, but not necessarily indecorous, occasion.”"

### Group J — Cross-cutting Providence Themes Building toward 50:20

### C-V2R5-61 | Providence trajectory in this range (pre-50:20)
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Across 37–43 Hamilton repeatedly frames events as divine guidance often concealed: non-theophanic destiny-dreams; Yahweh-with-Joseph in house and prison; dream-interpretations “belong to God”; double dream = certainty; brothers attribute money-find and distress to God while Joseph is instrument; steward’s “God put treasure”; El Shaddai’s mercy hoped; Manasseh/Ephraim theophoric naming. Explicit 45:5–8 and 50:20 cited as climax of Joseph’s own providential reading; 50:19 “not in place of God” anticipates distinction instrument ≠ deity.
- **Quote:** "The theme of providence emerges in two ways in Joseph’s life and in his own testimony. One is Joseph’s ability to interpret the happenings in his life and in that of his family as illustrative of God’s control and use of otherwise inscrutable events (45:5-8; 50:20). … Joseph is not himself God, as he asserts in 50:19, but he is God’s instrument."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 40:8; 42:28 (and cross-refs) / slice ~ll. 710–711, 1342–1344
- **Targets:** [[divine-providence]], [[joseph]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]]

### C-V2R5-62 | Source-critical restraint: literary unity preferred for 37, 39–41, 42–43
- **Claim (attributed Hamilton):** Consistently prefers narrative unity over J/E partitions for: Midianites/Ishmaelites (37); YHWH/Elohim distribution (39–41); prison status (39–40); one vs many officials / *ḥmš* (41); money discoveries (42); Judah-ch.43 sequel to Reuben-ch.42. Uses ANE and literary critics supporting unity.
- **Quote:** "Enough has been said to indicate that recourse to a J-E hypothesis, or to an original story with later redactional expansions, is not the only option in order to make sense of Gen. 37. … It appears to us that reading ch. 43 as a sequel to ch. 42 has less problems than reading it as a juxtaposition to ch. 42, and such an interpretation makes unnecessary the invention of an earlier but unmentioned trip by the brothers to Egypt."
- **Locus:** Comm. on 37:25–30; 43:3–5 / slice ~ll. 226, 1420–1421
